newsitem.title: CANADA: Quebec separatists struggle in Canada election.
newsitem.headline: Quebec separatists struggle in Canada election.

text.p: In the countdown to Canada's June 2 election, the separatist Bloc Quebecois is fighting to maintain its grip on French-speaking Quebec's secessionist heartland.

The Bloc has been hurt by its disorganized campaign start and the surging popularity of Quebec-born Conservative leader Jean Charest in this region of 300,000 people located 124 miles (200 km) north of the provincial capital Quebec City.

"There really has been a Jean Charest effect here and then there is Duceppe's disastrous campaign. He has made gaffe after gaffe," said Bertrand Genest, editor of the Chicoutimi daily newspaper Le Quotidien, referring to Bloc leader Gilles Duceppe.
A recent poll showed support for the Bloc at just 49 percent in the area's four electoral districts, down from the 67 percent it won in the 1993 federal election.
The Conservatives were at 29 percent. The Liberals of Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien -- a Quebecker, but unpopular in his home province -- were at 19 percent.
The situation is vastly different from the mood in October 1995, when separatists narrowly lost a referendum on Quebec independence and the Chicoutimi region voted 70 for sovereignty.
Two years earlier, in the 1993 federal election, the Bloc won 49 percent of the vote in Quebec, taking 54 of the province's 75 seats and becoming the official opposition in Canada's parliament.
The picturesque Chicoutimi region is 99 percent French-speaking and has a 17 percent unemployment rate, the highest of any urban area in Canada.
The region relies on heavy industry such as aluminum and pulp and paper making.
Faced with widespread voter apathy and rising Conservative support, the Bloc has been mobilizing to get its supporters to the polls.
In a speech on Tuesday in Quebec City, Quebec Premier Lucien Bouchard, who created the Bloc as a protest movement after he left the Conservative Party in 1990, exhorted separatist supporters to vote.
But some past Bloc voters were uncertain about their allegiance in interviews this week.
"Normally I would vote for the Bloc, but nowadays I don't know," said 27-year old school bus driver Dino Lapointe.

His wife Nancy Pageau, 23, who works in a local bar, was also wavering between the Bloc and the Conservatives. Pageau said she was once a staunch separatist but that recent trips to Western Canada changed her mind.
"By going there, I realized Quebec is a distinct society, but whether it will gain something from separation, I am not sure," she said.

"I will not vote for the Bloc because they talk too much about sovereignty instead of talking about our problems," said Martin Aube, a 23-year-old short-order cook who voted for separation in the 1995 referendum.
